title: A Systems Theory Approach to the Study of Colon and Lung Cancer Survivorship Using Novel Data Linkages
text: Cancer survivorship is significantly impacted by the utilization of novel and emerging cancer treatments. With this application, we will combine unique data sources to create a population-based cohort of men and women to examine targeted therapies, comorbidities, and multi-level contributors to survival for colon and lung cancers. We will convene an advisory board of community leaders, organizations, and clinicians to identify multi-level and modifiable targets for intervention.

title: Role of SMAD1/5/8 signaling in liver fibrosis
text:
Liver fibrosis is a serious health problem, which often progresses to cirrhosis and liver cancer, together
accounting for approximately 2 million deaths per year worldwide. New insights into the pathogenesis of liver
fibrosis in hemochromatosis and other liver disorders are needed to design novel therapeutic strategies.

title: Innate Immune Signal Transduction Specificity in Inflammatory Disease
text:
LAY SUMMARY
Overactivation of the inflammatory response underlies a multitude of inflammatory diseases, and the Abbott lab
attempts to identify novel proteins that can be targeted pharmaceutically to halt these diseases. To this end,
we have identified small molecule inhibitors of the kinase, RIPK2, a key inflammatory kinase. The current
application aims to extend this work by studying the kinase activity of RIPK2. Which proteins does it
phosphorylate? Which signaling pathways does it influence, and can we identify clinical scenarios in which its
inhibition would help ameliorate disease? Answers to these questions are important as our RIPK2 inhibitors
move into patients.

title: The role of development of glutamatergic inputs to the nucleus accumbens in adolescent behavior
text:
During adolescence, brain circuits critical for executive function, affective processing, and decision-making
undergo rapid and significant remodeling. Because of this development, adolescence is a common age for the
onset of neuropsychiatric disorders, thus, understanding the synaptic mechanisms that drive the neural circuits
for adolescent behavior is critical to ultimately improve neuropsychiatric health outcomes. By testing the central
hypothesis that synaptic maturation of specific glutamatergic inputs to the nucleus accumbens determines age-
specific sensitivity to aversive outcomes, this work will strengthen our understanding of the biological drivers of
adolescent behavior and provide potential avenues for mechanistic treatment of adolescent-onset
neuropsychiatric disorder.

title: Preclinical phenotypic modeling of chronic urologic pelvic pain
text:
The prevalence of urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome (UCPPS) in the United States is high, ranging from 14-
25% of men and women. The pathology of UCPPS is multifactorial and existing therapies are both limited and
unsatisfactory, underscoring the need for preclinical models that are reflective of disease complexity to advance
our mechanistic understanding and identify new treatment strategies. To achieve these goals, we propose to
systematically phenotype a dual-insult, preclinical model with high relevance to the clinical condition in order to
examine promising targetable units that individually or in combination alter the peripheral nervous system and
lead to UCPPS.

title: Advancing Cancer Control for Health and Value (ACCHV)
text: Cervical cancer burden represents a major burden of disease in the United States despite being largely avertable. Through mixed methods research to collect and analyze data on multi-level factors associated with cervical cancer prevention, this study seeks to identify how to achieve improvements in cancer control in the United States, including the potential to leverage innovative delivery approaches that have been successful in other settings.

title: The Effect of DDX41 Mutations on Hematopoiesis During Aging
text:
Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS) generally affect elderly people and are caused by acquired genetic defects
in blood stem cells, leading to loss of efficient blood production. Inherited mutations in DDX41 cause
predisposition to MDS by poorly understood mechanisms. In this project, we characterize samples from MDS
patients with DDX41 mutations to determine how the mutations affect the function of blood stem cells and then
use aged mice bearing the same DDX41 mutations to model the disease and test novel disease prevention
strategies.

title: Structural and dynamic traits underlying phenotypic variation in HIV-1 Env
text:
The HIV-1 Env glycoprotein mediates viral genome delivery into cells and is the sole target on the virus for
neutralizing antibodies. Despite recent advances in mapping its architecture, we lack a fundamental
understanding of Env structural variation among disparate isolates, which is the defining trait that makes HIV-1
a profound challenge for the immune system and for therapeutic development. The primary goals of the proposed
studies are to apply cryo-electron tomography and structural mass spectrometry to investigate the structural and
dynamic basis for isolate-specific differences in Env phenotypes in soluble ecotodomain and native virion-
displayed forms, and to dissect how neutralizing antibodies along the pathway to neutralization breadth gain the
ability to manage extreme Env variation.

title: ADAR mediated RNA editing is a causal mechanism in coronary artery disease
text:
Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, and from leveraging the power of
human genetics and mechanistic discovery, we are poised to understand causal mechanisms of disease and
design crucially needed therapies. In a groundbreaking discovery through complex disease genetics, RNA
editing of double stranded RNA, mediated by ADAR1, has been found to powerfully influence CAD risk. In this
proposal, I aim to understand the fundamental mechanisms of RNA editing and atherosclerosis, and further
define the potential for targeting the dsRNA sensor MDA5 for clinical therapy — allowing me to advance my
training and become an independent physician-scientist in cardiovascular medicine.

title: BMT Core: Southeast Bone Marrow Transplant Consortium
text:
Relevance
This project seeks to enroll patients onto clinical trials that explore strategies to improve outcomes
after hematopoietic stem cell transplant and genetically modified T cell therapies. Based in the Southeast, our
consortium will be important in enrolling increased numbers of minorities and rural individuals to these studies.
This application also proposes a clinical trial to directly compare outcomes of two currently-used methods to
reduce post-transplant graft-versus-host disease, to determine if one is more advantageous than the other.

title: High-throughput Phenotypic Screening
text: SUMMARY – High-throughput Phenotypic Screening (HPS) Core Modern biomedical technologies produce an unprecedented amount of data. Similarly, the number of small molecule compounds available for testing as potential therapeutics has increased exponentially in recent years. Sophisticated computational analysis methods, often leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning, parse these reams of possibilities into a smaller, but still substantial, number of predictions. This process produces an ever-expanding experimental “to do” list with respect to biological validation of the predictions made. To address this problem, we have established a versatile high-throughput screening facility. Importantly, our approach enables large-scale experimentation across a series of increasingly complex model systems, including cell cultures, human stem cell-derived organoids, and whole organisms. This allows the action of the tested gene or potential therapeutic to be assessed phenotypically, i.e., in terms of the desired physiological outcome, such as improved photoreceptor survival or function. Our new High-throughput Phenotypic Screening (HPS) Core is designed to enhance the ability of JHU/Wilmer vision researchers to fully leverage “big data” science and to test potential new therapeutics at unprecedented scales in living disease models. We anticipate that enabling comprehensive testing of the genes implicated in disease will allow entire gene regulatory networks underlying pathological conditions to be defined, and that performing large-scale drug discovery screens in increasingly complex disease models will advance our capacity to deliver promising therapeutics for sustaining, and even restoring, vision to our patients.

title: Data Science Core for Biomedical Research
text: DATA SCIENCE CORE FOR BIOMEDICAL RESEARCH: SUMMARY The Data Science (DS) Core serves as a centralized resource for providing expert and timely bioinformatics and other DS-related consulting, analysis, collaborative research, management, and training solutions for a broad range of high-throughput biomedical data. The DS Core will support the specific aims of HI-INBRE V by providing a strong and integrated DS service in research, education, investigation, and creation of innovative methodologies. During INBRE IV, the Bioinformatics Core made substantial progress to serve as a solid foundation for transition to the DS Core. We experienced an annual increase in the number of researchers utilizing the DS Core services from almost all the HI-INBRE institutions. The DS Core has successfully provided bioinformatics/biostatistics and other DS training and education opportunities to the HI-INBRE community. During INBRE IV, the core infrastructure was also significantly enhanced and several Ph.D. level data scientists were hired. The core has successfully contributed to peer-reviewed publications, grant applications and helped investigators to obtain a variety of research awards. In INBRE V, the DS Core will continue to function as an important component of the network. Specifically, the DS Core will contribute to INBRE V objectives in three key ways: (i) Customized Services: the DS Core will facilitate the acquisition of preliminary data for grant applications and subsequent research by HI-INBRE investigators via consultation on experimental design and data management as well as offer expertise in data analysis and interpretation; (ii) Education and Training: the DS Core will provide education in DS, as well as support career development for student and emerging faculty researchers, with special attention given for training DS skills to undergraduate students; (iii) Core Development: the DS Core will create tools and methods or repurpose existing tools and strategies to accelerate advances in the sciences. In all of these activities, the DS Core will work collaboratively with other local and national bioinformatics and DS cores. To reach these goals, we propose three Specific Aims: (1) Provide DS core services to support biomedical research needs of HI-INBRE investigators. (2) Meet the upskilling needs of biomedical faculty whose research is becoming increasing computationally intensive. (3) Enhance the biomedical DS pipeline in Hawaii. 1

title: Epithelial and Fibroblast Dysfunction in Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps
text: Project 2: Stromal Dysfunction in Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps Project Summary/Abstract Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is a common upper airway disease characterized by type 2 inflammation, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. These abnormalities are especially severe in patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD). Recent findings suggest that epithelial and stromal hyperactivation of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) contributes to epithelial hyperplasia, impaired differentiation, mesenchymal transition, and fibroblast and immunocyte activation. This project will define the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which mTORC1 signaling promotes persistent inflammation and polyp growth in CRSwNP. Aim 1 will delineate how mTORC1 hyperactivation disrupts epithelial repair and promotes ECM remodeling. Using primary basal cells and fibroblasts from CRSwNP patients, we will combine pharmacologic and CRISPR-based inhibition with single-cell RNA sequencing and functional assays to map how mTORC1 regulates epithelial proliferation, differentiation, EMT, and epithelial and fibroblast generation of soluble mediators and deposited EMM proteins. Aim 2 will investigate how ECM components activate mast cells (MCs) and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) through mechanoreceptors including integrins, Piezo1, and TRPV4. In vitro assays with human polyp- and PBMC-derived MCs/MDMs will assess cytokine, lipid mediator, and YAP signaling responses. In vivo, integrin αv will be conditionally deleted in MCs and macrophages using Cpa3Cre and Cx3cr1Cre mice in a murine model of ECM-rich allergic lung inflammation. Aim 3 will identify upstream ligands that drive epithelial mTORC1 activation in AERD and CRSwNP. Spatial transcriptomics and immune-epithelial co-culture systems will define which growth factors and cytokines drive epithelial mTOR activation and suppress PGE2. mTOR drivers and mTOR activity will be correlated with clinical outcomes in patient cohorts stratified by disease severity (fast versus slow polyp regrowth after endoscopic sinus surgery) or phenotype (AERD versus aspirin-tolerant controls), as well as in patients before or after treatment with dupilumab. This study will define a feed-forward circuit linking mTORC1, epithelial dysfunction, ECM remodeling, and immune activation, with the potential to guide new therapies for severe CRSwNP.

title: Understanding and controlling protein energy landscapes by combining simulations and experiments
text:
This MIRA proposal will provide fundamental insight into how myosin motors perform such an amazing diversity
of functions, from muscle contraction to hearing, using a combination of atomically-detailed computer simulations
and biophysical experiments. This insight will enable us to interpret genetic variation and design new myosin
variants and drug-like modulators of myosin function, thereby demonstrating our level of understanding and
laying a foundation for the future development of new therapeutics.

title: Impact of spatial and contextual factors on invasive fungal infection risk
text: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are a major public health concern, affecting 13 million people worldwide each year and leading to over 1.5 million deaths. Local contextual factors thought to be crucial risk factors for IFIs, particularly for molds and endemic fungi, but our ability to identify individuals at risk for or infected with IFIs is limited by our incomplete understanding of how specific spatial factors influence the distribution and spectrum of disease. This proposal is designed to elucidate the impact of spatial and contextual determinants on IFI risk and outcomes to improve prediction of and clinical care for IFIs.

title: Immunization against Multidrug-resistant Pathogens: Activating T Cell Immunity (IMPACT-CETR)
text:
The emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria represents the single greatest threat to our ability to treat
infectious diseases. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and MDR Gram-negative bacteria
such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae cause significant human morbidity and
mortality, and the Gram-negatives increasingly often possess such broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance that
there are very often few, or sometimes even no, available drugs to treat them. Broadly protective vaccines
against these pathogens would not only decrease the burden of infections but also lead to lower overall
antibiotic resistance due to less antibiotic use. This U19 proposal brings together investigators with wide and
synergistic expertise for vaccine development, including immunology, microbiology, bioinformatics, and animal
models of infection to develop and test new multicomponent vaccines that combine bacterial antigens to
stimulate multiple different types of immunity that can work together to give the best protection from infection.

title: Affective and Cognitive Mechanisms of Emotion-Based Impulsivity in Bipolar Disorder: Linking Neural Oscillatory Dynamics to Real-World Outcomes
text:
Projective Narrative
Emotion-based impulsivity, which involves difficulties with emotion regulation and cognitive control, is a
debilitating and understudied problem in bipolar spectrum disorders. This study will use advanced
neurophysiological measurement and ecological momentary assessment to examine whether neural
oscillations underlying response inhibition are associated with emotion regulation and impulsivity in daily life.
The resulting data may help to identify novel treatment targets for emotion-based impulsivity in bipolar
spectrum and related disorders.

title: Small Animal Imaging Facility (SAIF)
text: SMALL ANIMAL IMAGING FACILITY (SAIF) The Small Animal Imaging Facility (SAIF) advances cancer research by providing Cancer Center members with advanced imaging technologies and the expertise to successfully integrate imaging sciences into preclinical cancer research. SAIF provides comprehensive support for imaging services, including assistance in experimental design, development of specialty equipment, innovative imaging procedures, preparation and maintenance of animals for imaging, and data acquisition, processing, and analyses. SAIF maintains imaging labs on the North and South Campus (two different locations), to ensure broad access for Cancer Center members. SAIF possesses a variety of small animal imaging modalities, including Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), bioluminescence/fluorescence, micro-ultrasound, image guided radiation therapy, micro-Computed Tomography (microCT), Cryo-Fluorescence Tomography (CFT), Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP) and opto- acoustic imaging systems. Currently, SAIF has 24 imaging instruments optimized for small animals and a full complement of ancillary equipment to support animals before, during, and after imaging experiments. SAIF is also committed to community outreach and the education of CCSG members by hosting annual user meetings and by offering training and hosting symposia. During 2024, the SAIF supported 156 program members (91% of user base), supporting 231 peer-reviewed grants, involving investigators from all nine CCSG Research Programs (RPs). In 2024, SAIF supported 35 publications, of which 46% were in high-impact journals (Journal Impact Factor ≥10)). SAIF received strong institutional support, with $8.22M in capital equipment that complimented $1.57M in shared instrumentation grants. In the next funding cycle, we will expand and upgrade instrumentation to ensure broad access to instrumentation in mission-specific technologies. Specific Aims include 1) to maintain a broad range of state-of-the-art imaging instrumentation and dedicated staff; 2) to provide consultation, training, and support for acquisition and analysis of imaging data; and 3) to develop and implement new technologies and methods that enhance our ability to characterize cancer and response to therapy. A new magnetic particle imaging (MPI) device was recently installed in the SAIF that will expand our capabilities in theranostics and tracking cellular immunotherapy, and for exploring potential clinical applications. SAIF supports a comprehensive translational approach exemplified by the facilitation the development and preclinical evaluation of theranostic tracers and novel therapeutics, driven by collaborations with program members and the Radiotracer Production Facility. New instrumentation for simultaneous PET/MRI will enhance resources for assessing therapeutic delivery and characterizing response to therapy. We will continue to pursue artificial intelligence (AI) approaches for auto-segmentation and quantification of imaging data to support robust and reproducible image analysis.

title: Single-cell label-free identification of senescence by Raman microscopy and spatial genomics
text:
Single cell multi-omics profiling assays have opened new windows into understanding the properties, regulation,
dynamics, and function of senescence at unprecedented resolution and scale, however, these assays are
inherently destructive, precluding us from tracking the molecular profiles and dynamics of live cells in tissues,
whole organisms, or humans. We aim to develop an innovative technology “SenNetRaman” by combining the
recent advance in high-resolution and -speed Raman microscopy, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and
machine learning to unbiasedly map the spatially resolved biochemical and molecular signatures of senescent
cells. Overall, we believe “SenNetRaman” is highly modular and lays a foundation for future investigations into
exploring single-cell genome-wide molecular dynamics of senescent cells in tissues through imaging data, in
vitro, in vivo, and in humans.

title: Elasticity imaging of breast cancer during treatment
text:
Real-time elasticity-based imaging can be implemented for both diagnostic
imaging and therapeutics for monitoring tumor response to neo-adjuvant
chemotherapy and ultrasound thermal ablation. The techniques proposed stand
to enhance the current therapies available for breast cancer and ultimately have
a compatible imaging technique for treatment guidance of NACT, FUS or the
combination thereof.
